concepts_in_source_text_not_in_dataset: צְעָקָה בִּתְפִלָּה בְּפֶסַח (tze'akah ba-tefillah b'Pesach — crying out in prayer on Passover): Line 1 introduces the context that prayer on Pesach takes the form of crying out / beseeching. This is cited from the Targum on Lamentations 2:7 and the verse 'They gave voice in the House of God as on a festival day.' This is contextual/background, not a standalone bechina concept. Not in dataset.

מַצָּה (matzah — unleavened bread): Line 2 connects matzah to the verse 'tzedakah saves from death' (Proverbs 10:2) through the notarikon technique — the initials of מִמָּוֶת, צְדָקָה, תַּצִּיל (or the rearranged initials) spell מַצַּת. This establishes a letter-level allusion between charity and matzah, linking the Passover theme (matzah) to the spiritual protection offered by charity (matzah being the central symbol of Pesach liberation). This concept is not in the dataset. However, since the relationship is a notarikon/remez rather than an explicit bechina statement ('tzedakah IS matzah' using bechina language), this would not generate a bechina edge — it would be more appropriately recorded as an eitza or remez annotation if the data model supported that.

חֳלִי נוֹפֵל (choleh nofel — epilepsy / falling sickness): Line 3 gives the ailment for which the segulah (remedy) is prescribed. The node appears in the dataset as 'סגלה לחלי נופל רחמנא לצלן' (id 2303, reference 201, type eitza). The concept is thus already represented in the existing eitza edge, where spreading charity is the cause and the healing of epilepsy is the effect.

נֹפֵל מִן הַפָּסוּק (nofel from the verse — the acronym of Psalms 112:9): The initials of 'פִּזַּר נָתַן לָאֶבְיוֹנִים' (He scattered, he gave to the poor) = פ-נ-ל, which are rearranged to spell נ-פ-ל (nofel = falling). This notarikon technique proves the connection between charity and healing epilepsy. This is the proof-technique used within the existing eitza edge, not a separate bechina concept.
analysis_notes.gap_explanation: Torah #201 has no bechina edges in torahData.js. The source text is a three-line teaching with no bechina language. The teaching presents: (1) a contextual observation about Pesach prayer; (2) a notarikon connecting charity (צְדָקָה) to matzah (מַצָּה) via the initials of Proverbs 10:2; (3) a segulah: giving charity heals epilepsy (choleh nofel), proven via the acronym of Psalms 112:9. The only relationship in the dataset (edge 2303, type eitza) correctly captures the causal structure: litzedakah (giving charity) → heals choleh nofel. The notarikon connection between צְדָקָה and מַצָּה in line 2 is a letter-level allusion, not a bechina equation. The Rebbe does not declare 'charity IS matzah' in the sense of shared essential nature; he notes that the verse about charity contains the same letters as matzah — a remez pointing to Passover's spiritual unity of charity and liberation. Since the data model distinguishes only bechina (parallel essence) and eitza (cause-effect), and this notarikon relationship fits neither cleanly, it is most accurately described as exegetical context. No bechina edges are missing. The dataset's single eitza edge for Torah #201 accurately captures the sole causal relationship of this teaching.
analysis_notes.source_text_summary: Torah #201 is a three-part Passover-themed teaching. Part 1 (line 1): On Pesach, prayer takes the form of crying out (tze'akah), as alluded to in the Targum on Lamentations 2:7 interpreting the verse 'They gave voice in the House of God as on a festival day' as 'like the people praying on Passover.' Part 2 (line 2): The verse 'tzedakah saves from death' (Proverbs 10:2) contains the letters of מַצָּה (matzah) in its initials — linking Passover's central symbol to the spiritual protection of charity. Part 3 (line 3): Giving charity is a segulah (spiritual remedy) for epilepsy (choleh nofel); proof: the verse 'He scattered, he gave to the poor' (Psalms 112:9) has initials that spell נֹפֵל (falling/epilepsy). The entire teaching operates through notarikon (acronym technique) and a single eitza connection — there are no bechina (parallel-nature equivalence) relationships expressed anywhere in the text.
